item.title: ‘OnlyMarms’: Marmots Are on OnlyFans to Raise Money for Research
item.description: A team of scientists uploaded videos of the squirrel-like rodents in the wild on the adult-content site OnlyFans to raise money amid government budget cuts.
item.dc:creator: Emmett Lindner

item.title: On Second Test of Its Newest Starship Design, SpaceX Sticks the Landing
item.description: It was the 13th test overall of Starship. The success is a boon to NASA’s moon plans and SpaceX’s hopes to deploy a million data centers in orbit.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang

item.title: Can This New Enzyme Turn Back the Clock in Bodily Tissues?
item.description: In a recent study, scientists devised a way of reversing the buildup of compounds that lead to some age-related diseases.
item.dc:creator: K. R. Callaway

item.title: Life of Alan Turing Emerges in Richer Detail From Short Story
item.description: A Cambridge professor has transcribed a handwritten story that the famous mathematician wrote in the year before his death, presenting a different side of him.
item.dc:creator: Claire Moses
item.media:description: Sarah Dillon, a professor of English literature, with Alan Turing’s handwritten short story in the Archive Centre at King’s College, Cambridge.

item.title: Health Care Agency Discontinues Dozens of Active Research Awards
item.description: The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality slowed the awarding of new grants last year. Now it is stopping existing ones.
item.dc:creator: Katrina Miller
item.category: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
item.media:credit: Grant Hindsley for The New York Times
item.media:description: The Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, an arm of the Department of Health and Human Services, is a small agency that aims to make quality health care in the United States more affordable and accessible.

item.title: Four Young Mathematicians Receive Prestigious Fields Medals
item.description: The awards are bestowed only once every four years to mathematicians under the age of 40.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang

item.title: Jackie, Bald Eagle and Webcam Star, Is Recovering After an Attack in California
item.description: Jackie found an online audience through a webcam pointed at her nest in California. She was rescued last week after a fight with other eagles, officials said.
item.dc:creator: Alexandra E. Petri

item.title: What Were the Lotus-Eaters Eating in Homer’s ‘Odyssey’?
item.description: In Homer’s epic, Odysseus’s men eat something so powerful that they forget about home. Which plants could have produced such a soporific, narcotic and amnesiac effect?
item.dc:creator: Jack Truesdale
item.media:description: Blue lotus, Nymphaea caerulea, which botanists say is one plausible candidate for the plant that kept Odysseus’s men from wanting to leave the land of the lotus-eaters.

item.title: He’s the Last Great Land Artist You’ve Never Heard Of
item.description: Charles Ross spent 50 years building “Star Axis,” a naked-eye observatory in New Mexico. Now his masterwork is ready. How to share it with a changed world?
item.dc:creator: Travis Diehl and Brad Trone
item.category: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
item.media:credit: Charles Ross/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York
item.media:description: The Milky Way ribbons through the sky above “Star Axis.”

item.title: Paul Andrews, Founder of the Woodstock of U.F.O.s, Dies at 77
item.description: An annual convention in the California desert offered a safe space for believers to discuss extraterrestrial encounters, crop circles and other paranormal phenomena.
item.dc:creator: Michael S. Rosenwald

item.title: Guy Tudor, Whose Art Brought Obscure Birds to Life, Dies at 91
item.description: A self-taught ornithologist, he won a MacArthur fellowship for his precise, resplendent illustrations that appeared in definitive field guides to tropical songbirds.
item.dc:creator: Guy Trebay
item.category: MacArthur, John D and Catherine T, Foundation

item.title: What to Know About Peptides the FDA Is Considering for Use
item.description: The agency is considering whether compounding pharmacies should be allowed to produce BPC-157, TB-500 and other previously banned peptides.
item.dc:creator: Dana G. Smith

item.title: John Pardon Untangles the Theoretical Loops
item.description: The mathematics professor has won a prestigious Fields Medal for his work at the intersection of geometry, topology and physics.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang
item.category: State University of New York at Stony Brook

item.title: Jacob Tsimerman Lives in Number Theory
item.description: Dr. Tsimerman won one of four Fields Medals, an award for top mathematicians under 40, for his work on the André-Oort conjecture, but is now changing his focus to artificial intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang

item.title: Yu Deng Predicts the Actions of the Whole From Its Tiniest Parts
item.description: Dr. Deng, a mathematics professor at the University of Chicago, received a Fields Medal for his work on an equation describing fluid mechanics.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang

item.title: Hong Wang Twirls in Fractal Dimensions of Three
item.description: The young mathematician won a prestigious Fields Medal for her work on the so-called Kakeya conjecture.
item.dc:creator: Kenneth Chang

item.title: FDA Panel Supports Lifting Restrictions on Four Peptides
item.description: In an all-day hearing, the agency’s scientists argued against allowing broad access to unproven drugs that the agency had banned three years ago.
item.dc:creator: Christina Jewett and Dana G. Smith
item.media:description: Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. before a House Subcommittee on Health on Capitol Hill in April.

item.title: Should Travelers Give Up on Summer in Western Europe Because of the Heat?
item.description: A favorite vacation option may be at risk because of rising temperatures. Even those sticking with their summer plans agree: More air conditioning would help.
item.dc:creator: Tariro Mzezewa
item.media:credit: Dmitry Kostyukov for The New York Times
item.media:description: Seeking shade in the Place des Vosges in Paris during the June heat wave.

item.title: How to Eat a 2,000-Pound Fish? These Orcas Choose to Pulverize It.
item.description: Marine biologists in Mexico captured video of a strange maneuver that killer whales used to shred their meal.
item.dc:creator: Alexa Robles-Gil

item.title: Dunes Sagebrush Lizard Stripped of Endangered Status by Judge
item.description: The dunes sagebrush lizard, found only in the oil-rich Permian Basin, was classified as endangered two years ago.
item.dc:creator: Catrin Einhorn and Maxine Joselow
item.media:description: The dunes sagebrush lizard is found only in areas of the Permian Basin in southeast New Mexico and West Texas.

item.title: Deep in This Lake, a Contagious Cancer Is Spreading
item.description: Transmissible tumors have been reported in a handful of animal species, but never before among fish. Is it possible in humans?
item.dc:creator: Carl Zimmer

item.title: What the Cyclospora Outbreak Reveals
item.description: Warming is expected to fuel the spread of food-borne pathogens. We might not be prepared.
item.dc:creator: Claire Brown
item.media:description: A microscopic view of cyclospora parasite eggs, stained reddish pink, in a lab sample.

item.title: Monkeys Understand Shapes in Almost the Same Way as Humans
item.description: Our geometric intuition, long considered something that sets us apart, seems to be shared with other primates.
item.dc:creator: K. R. Callaway
item.category: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

item.title: Susumu Tonegawa Dies at 86; Nobel Laureate Showed How Antibodies Fight Infection
item.description: The first Japanese scientist to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, he went on to discover how memories are stored, advancing understanding of how the brain works.
item.dc:creator: Dylan Loeb McClain
item.media:description: Susumu Tonegawa in 2005. “Few scientists have reshaped our understanding of biology as profoundly,” Myriam Heiman, the director of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory at M.I.T., said.

item.title: Cameron Hamilton Poised to Lead FEMA Once More
item.description: Cameron Hamilton defended the agency last year when President Trump talked about eliminating it. Emergency managers hope for more stability if he’s confirmed as administrator.
item.dc:creator: Scott Dance
item.media:description: Just over a year after being fired, Cameron Hamilton is on the brink of assuming the helm of FEMA once again.

item.title: 1,700 H.I.V. Treatment Sites Closed After Trump Aid Cuts, a Study Finds

President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief

item.title: The U.S. Is Pulling Back on Energy Efficiency
item.description: The Trump administration is undoing fuel-saving efforts even as war in Iran, data centers and heat waves are pushing up gasoline and electricity costs.
item.dc:creator: Brad Plumer
item.media:description: A dishwasher at a General Electric plant in Louisville, Ky. The Energy Department has moved to repeal 17 standards for dishwashers, washing machines, kitchen appliances and more.

item.title: Trump Attacks National Academies Over Climate Chapter in Judges’ Manual
item.description: The president joined Republican officials who slammed the National Academies of Sciences for a chapter about climate science in an educational guide for judges.

item.media:description: The National Academies of Sciences building in Washington, D.C.

item.title: The Sewer Knows What You Ate
item.description: During the Covid-19 pandemic, wastewater testing became a virus warning system. Now, scientists are using the approach to understand how communities eat.
item.dc:creator: Simar Bajaj
item.category: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

item.title: The Best Genetic Risk Tools Don’t Work Equally for Everyone
item.description: Genetic prediction models are poised to revolutionize medicine. But because they have been trained on European DNA, they threaten to widen health care disparities.
item.dc:creator: Emily Baumgaertner Nunn
